question_html: As per section 2(5) of the CGST Act, 'agent' means a person, including a factor, broker, commission agent, arhatia, del credere agent, an auctioneer or any other mercantile agent, by whatever name called, who:

options.A: Carries on the business of supply or receipt of goods or services or both on behalf of another
options.B: Carries on the business of supply or receipt of goods or services or both exclusively on his own account, without any reference to another person

options.D: Provides only advisory or consultancy services relating to the supply of goods or services, without ever taking part in the actual supply or receipt

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) Carries on the business of supply or receipt of goods or services or both on behalf of another

As per section 2(5), 'agent' means a person, including a factor, broker, commission agent, arhatia, del credere agent, an auctioneer or any other mercantile agent, by whatever name called, who carries on the business of supply or receipt of goods or services or both on behalf of another.

question_html: As per section 2(31) of the CGST Act, 'consideration' in relation to the supply of goods or services or both includes any payment made or to be made, and the monetary value of any act or forbearance, in respect of, in response to, or for the inducement of the supply, whether by the recipient or by any other person, but SHALL NOT include:

options.A: Any payment made by the recipient in a currency other than Indian Rupees, since only INR payments qualify as consideration
options.B: Any subsidy given by the Central Government or a State Government
options.C: Any deposit given in respect of the supply, even where the supplier subsequently applies such deposit as consideration for the supply
options.D: Any act or forbearance rendered by the recipient personally, as opposed to a third party, since only third-party acts qualify as consideration

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) Any subsidy given by the Central Government or a State Government

As per section 2(31), 'consideration' includes any payment made or to be made (whether in money or otherwise) and the monetary value of any act or forbearance, in respect of, in response to, or for the inducement of the supply, whether by the recipient or by any other person - but shall NOT include any subsidy given by the Central Government or a State Government. A deposit is not considered as payment unless the supplier applies it as consideration for the supply.

question_html: As per section 2(75) of the CGST Act, 'money' means Indian legal tender or any foreign currency, cheque, promissory note, bill of exchange, letter of credit, draft, pay order, traveller cheque, money order, postal or electronic remittance, or any other RBI-recognised instrument, when used as a consideration to settle an obligation or exchange with Indian legal tender of another denomination, but SHALL NOT include:

options.A: Any cheque or promissory note, since these are treated as separate financial instruments rather than as 'money' for GST purposes
options.B: Any postal or electronic remittance, since only physical currency notes and coins qualify as 'money' under the definition
options.C: Foreign currency of any kind, since 'money' under GST is restricted exclusively to Indian legal tender
options.D: Any currency that is held for its numismatic value

answer_html:
Correct answer: (D) Any currency that is held for its numismatic value

As per section 2(75), 'money' includes Indian legal tender, foreign currency, and various recognised financial instruments when used as consideration to settle an obligation or exchange with Indian legal tender of another denomination, but shall NOT include any currency that is held for its numismatic value (i.e. as a collector's item rather than as a medium of exchange).

question_html: As per the proviso to section 2(105) of the CGST Act, a person who organises or arranges, directly or indirectly, the supply of specified actionable claims (including a person who owns, operates or manages a digital or electronic platform for such supply) shall be:

options.A: Deemed to be the supplier of such actionable claims, whether such actionable claims are supplied by him or through him, and whether consideration (including virtual digital assets) is paid or conveyed to him or through him or placed at his disposal in any manner
options.B: Treated as a mere intermediary who bears no liability under GST law, since the actual supplier of the actionable claims remains solely liable to pay tax
options.C: Required to obtain a distinct registration as a 'platform operator' separate from his registration as a supplier of goods or services
options.D: Liable to pay GST only on the platform facilitation fee, with the underlying value of the actionable claims falling outside the scope of his liability

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) Deemed to be the supplier of such actionable claims, whether such actionable claims are supplied by him or through him, and whether consideration (including virtual digital assets) is paid or conveyed to him or through him or placed at his disposal in any manner

As per the proviso to section 2(105), a person who organises or arranges, directly or indirectly, supply of specified actionable claims, including a person who owns, operates or manages a digital or electronic platform for such supply, shall be deemed to be a supplier of such actionable claims - all provisions of the Act apply to such person as if he is the supplier liable to pay tax in relation to such supply.

question_html: As per section 15(1) of the CGST Act, the value of a supply of goods or services or both shall be the transaction value, which is the price actually paid or payable for the said supply, PROVIDED that:

options.A: The supply is made exclusively to a Government entity, and the recipient has obtained prior approval of the jurisdictional GST officer
options.B: The supplier and the recipient of the supply are not related, and the price is the sole consideration for the supply
options.C: The supplier and recipient are related persons, and the price has been certified by an independent valuer appointed under the Companies Act, 2013
options.D: The supply is made under a written contract of at least twelve months' duration, and price is one of several forms of consideration for the supply

answer_html:

subject: Goods and Services Tax
question_html: Wholesale price for 1 MT of a commodity sold by Vishesh Industries in the ordinary course of business is Rs. 8,500. However, Vishesh Industries sells 1 MT of the same commodity to an unrelated customer, Nikhil Traders, for Rs. 8,000. What is the value of supply made by Vishesh Industries to Nikhil Traders?

options.A: Rs. 8,500, being the wholesale price charged by Vishesh Industries in the ordinary course of its business
options.B: The average of Rs. 8,500 and Rs. 8,000, i.e. Rs. 8,250, as a blended value for GST purposes
options.C: Rs. 8,000, being the price actually paid or payable for the specific supply being valued, and not the general wholesale price
options.D: Rs. 8,500, since GST law mandates the use of the higher of the wholesale price or the actual transaction price

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) Rs. 8,000, being the price actually paid or payable for the specific supply being valued, and not the general wholesale price

Under section 15(1), the transaction value is the price actually paid or payable for the SPECIFIC supply being valued - it includes the amount already paid and the amount payable (agreed to be paid), and is not to be confused with a general wholesale or list price. Here, the value of supply to Nikhil Traders is Rs. 8,000, the price actually paid/payable for that specific transaction, not the Rs. 8,500 wholesale price.

subject: Goods and Services Tax
question_html: Under section 15(1), the word 'payable' in the phrase 'price actually paid or payable' refers to:

options.A: Only amounts that have already been physically received by the supplier at the time of valuation, excluding any outstanding agreed price
options.B: The maximum retail price (MRP) printed on the goods, regardless of the actual price agreed between the parties
options.C: The price as revised after any post-supply price negotiation between the supplier and recipient, applied retrospectively to the original transaction
options.D: The price that is agreed to be paid for the goods or services, including amounts not yet paid at the time the supply is being valued for tax

answer_html:
Correct answer: (D) The price that is agreed to be paid for the goods or services, including amounts not yet paid at the time the supply is being valued for tax

The transaction value under section 15(1) is the price for the specific supply being valued - it includes the amount already paid at the time the supply is being valued for tax, as well as the amount payable (i.e. agreed to be paid) and not yet paid at that time. The word 'payable' refers to the price that is agreed to be paid for the goods/services.

question_html: As per the Explanation to section 15, persons shall be deemed to be 'related persons' if, among other criteria:

options.A: Such persons are officers or directors of one another's businesses, or such persons are legally recognised partners in business
options.B: Such persons have, at any point in time, entered into a single commercial transaction with each other, regardless of any ongoing relationship

question_html: As per the Explanation to section 15, persons shall be deemed to be 'related persons' if any person directly or indirectly owns, controls or holds a specified percentage or more of the outstanding voting stock or shares of both of them. What is this specified percentage?

options.A: 10% or more, mirroring the threshold commonly used for 'significant beneficial ownership' under company law

As per the Explanation to section 15, persons are deemed to be related if any person directly or indirectly owns, controls or holds twenty-five per cent (25%) or more of the outstanding voting stock or shares of both of them.

options.A: One of them directly or indirectly controls the other, or both of them are directly or indirectly controlled by a third person
options.B: Together they directly or indirectly control a third person
options.C: Such persons have jointly bid for and won the same Government tender within the preceding financial year

answer_html:

question_html: As per the Explanation to section 15, persons who are associated in the business of one another in that one is the sole agent, sole distributor or sole concessionaire (howsoever described) of the other:

options.A: Shall never be treated as related persons under any circumstances, since a sole agency/distributorship arrangement is, by its nature, a principal-to-principal commercial relationship
options.B: Shall be deemed related only if the sole agency/distributorship arrangement has continued for more than five years
options.C: Shall be deemed related only if the sole agent/distributor/concessionaire directly or indirectly holds 25% or more of the voting stock of the other

question_html: A supplier of goods pays municipal tax in relation to the goods being supplied and charges the same separately from the recipient. How is this municipal tax treated for the purpose of determining the value of supply?

options.A: It is excluded from the value of supply, since municipal taxes are local-body levies and are therefore outside the scope of section 15(2)(a) entirely
options.B: It forms part of the value of supply, since it is a tax levied under a law other than the GST laws and is charged separately by the supplier [Section 15(2)(a)]
options.C: It is included in the value of supply only if the municipal tax exceeds 5% of the base price of the goods
options.D: It is excluded from the value of supply only if it is separately disclosed on a separate invoice rather than the main tax invoice

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) It forms part of the value of supply, since it is a tax levied under a law other than the GST laws and is charged separately by the supplier [Section 15(2)(a)]

As per section 15(2)(a), all taxes, duties, cesses, fees and charges levied under any law other than the GST laws are includible in the value of supply if charged separately by the supplier. In effect, all taxes/duties not subsumed in GST form part of the taxable value for GST purposes. Since the municipal tax is charged separately here, it forms part of the value of supply.

question_html: As clarified by the CBIC vide Circular No. 76/50/2018 GST dated 31.12.2018 (amended vide corrigendum dated 07.03.2019), tax collected at source (TCS) under the provisions of the Income-tax Act, 1961 is:

options.A: Includible in the value of supply for GST purposes under section 15(2)(a), on par with other non-GST taxes charged separately
options.B: Includible in the value of supply only where the recipient is an individual, but excludible where the recipient is a body corporate

question_html: What is the stated rationale, per Circular No. 76/50/2018 GST, for TCS under the Income-tax Act, 1961 NOT being included in the value of supply for GST purposes?

options.A: TCS is an interim levy that does not have the character of a tax (it is essentially a mechanism for collection of income-tax in advance, adjustable against the ultimate income-tax liability of the buyer)
options.B: TCS is levied only on services and not on goods, and section 15(2)(a) applies exclusively to levies on goods
options.C: TCS is levied by local authorities rather than by the Central or State Government, placing it outside the scope of section 15(2)(a) altogether
options.D: TCS is always charged inclusive of GST by the supplier, making a separate inclusion under section 15(2)(a) unnecessary to avoid double counting

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) TCS is an interim levy that does not have the character of a tax (it is essentially a mechanism for collection of income-tax in advance, adjustable against the ultimate income-tax liability of the buyer)

Circular No. 76/50/2018 GST clarifies that TCS under the Income-tax Act, 1961 would not be includible in the value of supply for GST purposes because it is an interim levy not having the character of a tax - unlike other non-GST taxes/duties/cesses which ARE includible under section 15(2)(a) when charged separately.

subject: Goods and Services Tax
question_html: Grand Biz contracts with ABC Co. to conduct a dealers' meet. In furtherance of this, Grand Biz separately contracts with a soft drinks vendor to deliver soft drinks at the venue; Grand Biz is contractually liable to make this payment. However, the soft drinks vendor wants payment upon delivery, so ABC Co. directly pays the soft drinks vendor's bill upon receiving the crates. This amount is not billed by Grand Biz to ABC Co. How is this amount treated for GST valuation purposes?

options.A: It is excluded from the value of supply entirely, since it was never billed by Grand Biz to ABC Co. and thus falls outside the scope of the transaction altogether
options.B: It is treated as a wholly separate and independent supply made directly by the soft drinks vendor to ABC Co., with no bearing whatsoever on the value of supply between Grand Biz and ABC Co.
options.C: It is included in the value of supply only if Grand Biz subsequently reimburses ABC Co. for the amount paid to the soft drinks vendor
options.D: It is added to the value of supply provided by Grand Biz to ABC Co. for payment of GST, since it is an amount Grand Biz was contractually liable to pay but which was instead incurred directly by ABC Co. (the recipient) [Section 15(2)(b)]

answer_html:
Correct answer: (D) It is added to the value of supply provided by Grand Biz to ABC Co. for payment of GST, since it is an amount Grand Biz was contractually liable to pay but which was instead incurred directly by ABC Co. (the recipient) [Section 15(2)(b)]

Since Grand Biz was contractually liable to make the payment to the soft drinks vendor (as part of its arrangement for the dealers' meet), but ABC Co. (the recipient) directly discharged this liability, the amount is added to the value of supply provided by Grand Biz to ABC Co. for payment of GST, as per section 15(2)(b) - even though it was never billed by Grand Biz itself.

question_html: Which of the following statements about commission and packing charges is correct, as per the analysis of section 15(2)(c)?

options.A: Commission and packing charges are excluded from the value of supply in all cases, since they are treated as post-supply administrative costs rather than part of the consideration
options.B: Commission paid to an agent and recovered from the buyer of the goods/services forms part of the value of supply, and packing charges, if charged by the supplier to the recipient, are similarly part of the value of supply
options.C: Commission is includible in the value of supply, but packing charges are excludible regardless of whether they are charged to the recipient

subject: Goods and Services Tax
question_html: Sapiant Ltd. supplies machinery to Chandra Ltd. and charges, apart from the price of the machinery, associated handling and loading charges, and installation and commissioning charges at the recipient's site. How should these charges be treated for GST valuation purposes?

options.A: Only the handling and loading charges are includible in the value; installation and commissioning charges are excludible since they occur after the machinery has already been delivered to the recipient's premises
options.B: Both categories of charges are excludible from the value of supply, since section 15(2)(c) applies exclusively to commission and packing and does not extend to installation or handling charges
options.C: Both the handling/loading charges and the installation/commissioning charges are includible in the value of supply, being amounts charged for something done by the supplier in respect of the supply at the time of, or before, delivery/completion of the supply [Section 15(2)(c)]
options.D: Only the installation and commissioning charges are includible; handling and loading charges are excludible since they are incurred before, rather than at, the time of supply

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) Both the handling/loading charges and the installation/commissioning charges are includible in the value of supply, being amounts charged for something done by the supplier in respect of the supply at the time of, or before, delivery/completion of the supply [Section 15(2)(c)]

Installation and testing charges at the recipient's site are added to the value, being an amount charged for something done by the supplier in respect of the supply at the time of making the supply. Similarly, handling/loading charges (weighment, loading charges, designing charges etc.) incurred before/at the time of supply are added to the value, if billed to the recipient. Both categories are includible under section 15(2)(c).

question_html: AKJ Foods Pvt. Ltd. receives an order for supply of processed food, and the customer wants the consignment tested for gluten and specified chemical residues. AKJ Foods Pvt. Ltd. conducts the testing before the supply and charges a separate testing fee from the customer. AKJ Foods Pvt. Ltd. argues that the testing fee should not form part of the consideration, being a separate activity. Is this argument correct?

options.A: Yes - testing is a distinct service unrelated to the supply of processed food, and hence the testing fee is validly excluded from the value of the underlying supply
options.B: Yes - since the testing fee is separately invoiced from the price of the processed food, it is automatically excluded from the value of supply under section 15(3)
options.C: No - but only because the testing was mandated by the customer's own specifications, rather than because of any general rule under section 15(2)(c)
options.D: No - as per section 15(2)(c), the amount charged for anything done by the supplier in respect of the supply at the time of, or before, delivery of goods is includible in the value of supply, and since the testing is done before delivery, the testing fee must be included

answer_html:
Correct answer: (D) No - as per section 15(2)(c), the amount charged for anything done by the supplier in respect of the supply at the time of, or before, delivery of goods is includible in the value of supply, and since the testing is done before delivery, the testing fee must be included

Section 15(2)(c) specifies that the amount charged for anything done by the supplier in respect of the supply at the time of or before delivery of goods or supply of services shall be included in the value of supply. Since AKJ Foods Pvt. Ltd. does the testing before delivery of the goods, the testing charges must be included in the value of the supply - the company's argument that it is a separate activity is not correct.

question_html: Where the supplier agrees to deliver goods at the buyer's premises and arranges for transport and insurance, how are the outward freight and transit insurance charges treated for GST valuation?

options.A: The contract of supply becomes a composite supply (the principal supply being the supply of goods), and outward freight and transit insurance become part of the value of the composite supply, with GST payable thereon at the same rate as applicable for the relevant goods
options.B: Outward freight and transit insurance are always treated as a wholly separate and independently taxable supply of transportation/insurance services, taxed at the GST rate applicable to GTA/insurance services
options.C: Outward freight and transit insurance are excluded from the value of supply of goods in every case, regardless of whether the supplier or the buyer bears these costs
options.D: Outward freight is includible in the value of supply, but transit insurance is always excludible, since insurance is treated as a distinct exempt supply under GST law

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) The contract of supply becomes a composite supply (the principal supply being the supply of goods), and outward freight and transit insurance become part of the value of the composite supply, with GST payable thereon at the same rate as applicable for the relevant goods

Where the supplier agrees to deliver the goods at the buyer's premises and arranges for transport and insurance, the contract of supply becomes a composite supply, with the principal supply being the supply of goods. Therefore, outward freight and transit insurance become part of the value of the composite supply, and GST is payable thereon at the same rate as applicable for the relevant goods.

question_html: If the contract for supply of goods is on an EX-FACTORY basis, where the buyer itself arranges and pays for the outward freight and insurance, how is this freight/insurance treated for the purpose of valuing the supply of goods?

options.A: It will still be included in the value of supply of goods, since freight and insurance are always part of a composite supply irrespective of who arranges or bears the cost
options.B: It will NOT be included in the value of supply of goods, since the supplier neither arranges nor charges for the freight/insurance under an ex-factory arrangement
options.C: It will be included in the value of supply of goods only if the buyer subsequently seeks reimbursement of the freight cost from the supplier
options.D: It will be treated as a separate residual supply taxable at a notified rate under section 15(5), regardless of the ex-factory nature of the contract

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) It will NOT be included in the value of supply of goods, since the supplier neither arranges nor charges for the freight/insurance under an ex-factory arrangement

If the contract for supply is on an ex-factory basis, where the buyer pays the outward freight and insurance (arranging for it independently), this amount will NOT be included in the value of supply of goods - this is distinct from a situation where the supplier itself agrees to deliver at the buyer's premises and arranges for transport/insurance, which creates a composite supply.

question_html: As per section 15(2)(d) of the CGST Act, the value of supply shall include:

options.A: Interest or late fee or penalty only where such amounts are expressly quantified in the original tax invoice for the underlying supply
options.B: Interest for delayed payment of consideration for goods, but NOT for services, since section 15(2)(d) is expressly restricted to supplies of goods
options.C: Interest or late fee or penalty for delayed payment of any consideration for any supply
options.D: Only penalty amounts, with interest and late fees for delayed payment being excluded from the value of supply under a separate, standalone provision

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) Interest or late fee or penalty for delayed payment of any consideration for any supply

As per section 15(2)(d), the value of a supply shall include interest or late fee or penalty for delayed payment of any consideration for any supply (of goods or services) - the value includes not only the base price but also the charges for delay in payment.

question_html: A supply priced at Rs. 3,000 is made, with a credit period of 1 month for payment. Thereafter, interest at 12% p.a. is chargeable. Payment is received after the lapse of two months from the date of supply (i.e. one month after the credit period expires). What is the value of supply, assuming the interest is exclusive of GST?

options.A: Rs. 3,000, since interest for delayed payment is never includible in the value of supply under any circumstances
options.B: Rs. 3,360, computed as 12% p.a. interest on Rs. 3,000 for the entire two-month period from the date of supply, without regard to the free credit period
options.C: Rs. 3,000, with the interest being taxed as an entirely separate, independent supply of a financial service
options.D: Rs. 3,030 (Rs. 3,000 base price plus Rs. 30 interest, being 12% p.a., i.e. 1% per month, on Rs. 3,000 for the one month of delay beyond the free credit period)

answer_html:
Correct answer: (D) Rs. 3,030 (Rs. 3,000 base price plus Rs. 30 interest, being 12% p.a., i.e. 1% per month, on Rs. 3,000 for the one month of delay beyond the free credit period)

Interest at 12% p.a. (i.e. 1% per month) on Rs. 3,000 for one month of delay after the free credit period of one month is Rs. 30. Such interest is added to the value under section 15(2)(d), so the value of supply works out to Rs. 3,030 (assuming the interest is exclusive of GST).

subject: Goods and Services Tax
question_html: The selling price of a notebook is Rs. 60. For notebooks sold to students in Government schools, a company receives a price-linked subsidy of Rs. 35 per notebook from an NGO, so that students pay only Rs. 25 per notebook. What is the value of the notebook for GST purposes?

options.A: Rs. 25, being only the amount actually paid by the students, since the subsidy is provided for a genuinely charitable/educational purpose
options.B: Rs. 60, but this would instead be Rs. 25 if the very same subsidy were granted by the Central or State Government, since Government subsidies are also includible in the value of supply
options.C: Rs. 60, being the full price inclusive of the non-Government subsidy, since a subsidy from a non-Government body that is directly linked to price IS includible in the value of supply
options.D: Rs. 35, being the amount of the subsidy alone, treated as the taxable value of a separate and independent supply made by the NGO

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) Rs. 60, being the full price inclusive of the non-Government subsidy, since a subsidy from a non-Government body that is directly linked to price IS includible in the value of supply

Since the subsidy of Rs. 35 is given by a non-Government body (the NGO) and is directly linked to the price of the notebook, it is includible in the value of supply under section 15(2)(e). Therefore, the value of the notebook is Rs. 60 (Rs. 25 paid by the student plus Rs. 35 subsidy). question_html: Royal Biscuit Co. gives a discount of 30% on the list price to its distributors. For a carton of biscuits, the tax invoice mentions a list price of Rs. 300, on which the 30% discount is applied to arrive at the final invoiced price. What is the value of supply?

options.B: Rs. 90, being only the amount of the discount, treated as a separate deemed supply for GST purposes
options.C: Rs. 210, but only if the distributor subsequently reverses input tax credit proportionate to the discount, mirroring the post-supply discount conditions
options.D: Rs. 210 (Rs. 300 less 30% discount of Rs. 90), since the discount is allowed at the time of supply and is shown in the invoice [Section 15(3)(a)]

answer_html:
Correct answer: (D) Rs. 210 (Rs. 300 less 30% discount of Rs. 90), since the discount is allowed at the time of supply and is shown in the invoice [Section 15(3)(a)]

Since the discount of 30% is allowed at the time of supply and is shown/recorded in the invoice, it satisfies section 15(3)(a), and the value of supply is the final invoiced price after discount: Rs. 300 - Rs. 90 = Rs. 210. (Note: for pre-supply/at-supply discounts recorded in the invoice, there is no requirement for the recipient to reverse any ITC - that condition applies only to post-supply discounts under section 15(3)(b).)

question_html: Why can a cash discount offered for making payment within a stipulated time typically NOT be recorded in the invoice at the time of supply, even though the discount terms may exist at that time?

options.A: Because cash discounts are, as a category, categorically prohibited from being recorded on tax invoices under the CGST Rules
options.B: Because the supplier does not know, at the time of supply, whether the buyer will actually make the payment within the stipulated time, so the discount cannot be quantified and recorded on the invoice at that stage
options.C: Because recording a cash discount on the invoice would automatically disqualify the supplier from claiming any input tax credit on its own inward supplies
options.D: Because cash discounts must always be routed through a separate commercial credit note rather than through the original tax invoice, regardless of timing

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) Because the supplier does not know, at the time of supply, whether the buyer will actually make the payment within the stipulated time, so the discount cannot be quantified and recorded on the invoice at that stage

It is not always commercially feasible to determine all discounts before or at the time of supply or record them in the invoice. For a cash discount given for payment within a stipulated time, even though the discount terms are established before/at the time of supply, the supplier does not know at that stage whether the buyer will actually pay within the stipulated time - so the discount cannot be recorded in the invoice, and it is instead passed on subsequently via a credit note if the conditions of section 15(3)(b) are met.

question_html: Pink and Blue Pvt. Ltd. (PBPL) sold goods to Orange Pvt. Ltd. (OPL), with the contract stipulating a 2% discount if OPL pays within one month. OPL avails input tax credit on the full invoice value and makes payment within the stipulated period. PBPL then issues a credit note for the discount value plus proportionate GST. What must OPL do upon receiving this credit note, for PBPL to be entitled to reduce its output tax liability by the GST component of the discount?

options.A: OPL need not take any action at all, since PBPL's entitlement to reduce its output tax liability arises automatically upon merely issuing the credit note
options.B: OPL must instead pay the GST component of the credit note in cash to the Government directly, bypassing any adjustment to its input tax credit
options.C: OPL must reverse the input tax credit attributable to the discount (i.e. the GST component of the credit note), consequent to which PBPL's output tax liability is correspondingly reduced
options.D: OPL must cancel and reissue its original purchase invoice to reflect the discounted price, in addition to any adjustment relating to input tax credit

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) OPL must reverse the input tax credit attributable to the discount (i.e. the GST component of the credit note), consequent to which PBPL's output tax liability is correspondingly reduced

As per section 15(3)(b), since the discount is established in terms of a pre-existing agreement and can be linked to the relevant invoice, it is deductible from the value of supply PROVIDED the recipient (OPL) reverses the input tax credit attributable to the discount, based on the document (credit note) issued by the supplier (PBPL). Only upon such reversal by OPL can PBPL correspondingly reduce its own output tax liability by the same amount.

options.B: Yes - since the insurance company pre-discloses the availability of the NCB discount (subject to conditions) in the policy document itself, and also specifically mentions the NCB discount in the invoice, this is in consonance with the conditions for deduction of a discount under section 15(3)(a), and NCB is therefore a permissible deduction
options.C: No - NCB can never qualify under section 15(3)(a) because its precise quantum is known only at the time of policy renewal, which is necessarily after the time of the original supply of insurance services
options.D: Yes - but only where the insured has not made any claims for a minimum of five consecutive policy years, regardless of whether the NCB is disclosed in the policy document or invoice

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) Yes - since the insurance company pre-discloses the availability of the NCB discount (subject to conditions) in the policy document itself, and also specifically mentions the NCB discount in the invoice, this is in consonance with the conditions for deduction of a discount under section 15(3)(a), and NCB is therefore a permissible deduction

As clarified vide Circular No. 186/18/2022 GST, since insurance companies pre-disclose the availability of NCB (subject to conditions) in the policy document itself and also specifically mention the NCB discount in the invoice, this satisfies the conditions laid down for deduction of a discount under section 15(3)(a) (discount given before/at the time of supply and recorded in the invoice). NCB is therefore a permissible deduction under section 15(3)(a) for valuing insurance services.

question_html: Where the deduction on account of No Claim Bonus (NCB) is provided in the invoice issued by an insurer to the insured, on what amount is GST leviable, per Circular No. 186/18/2022 GST?

options.A: GST shall be leviable on the gross premium amount before deduction of the NCB, with the NCB itself being separately reversed by the insured as an ITC adjustment
options.B: GST shall be leviable on the average of the gross premium and the net (post-NCB) premium, as a blended base for computing the tax liability

question_html: As per section 15(4) of the CGST Act, where sub-section (1) is not applicable - i.e. where the transaction is with a related party, and/or price is not the sole consideration for the supply of goods/services - the value shall be determined:

options.A: At NIL value in every such case, since section 15(1) is the exclusive basis for valuation of any taxable supply under GST law

question_html: As per the amendment proposed to section 15(3)(b) vide the Finance Act, 2026, once such amendment comes into effect, what change is proposed to the conditions for excluding a post-supply discount from the value of supply?

options.A: It does away with the requirement of ITC reversal by the recipient altogether, so that any post-supply discount evidenced by a credit note under section 34 would automatically be excludible from the value of supply
options.B: It does away with the requirement of linking the post-supply discount to an agreement entered into at or before the time of supply and capable of being linked invoice-wise - instead, such discount will be excluded from the value of supply if the supplier issues a credit note under section 34 and the recipient reverses the proportionate input tax credit
options.C: It extends the existing twin-condition test (pre-existing agreement plus ITC reversal) to pre-supply discounts under section 15(3)(a) as well, aligning the treatment of both categories of discount
options.D: It removes discounts from the scope of section 15(3) altogether, treating all discounts (pre-supply and post-supply alike) as a matter to be governed exclusively by the valuation rules under Chapter IV of the CGST Rules

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) It does away with the requirement of linking the post-supply discount to an agreement entered into at or before the time of supply and capable of being linked invoice-wise - instead, such discount will be excluded from the value of supply if the supplier issues a credit note under section 34 and the recipient reverses the proportionate input tax credit

As per the Finance Act, 2026 amendment (not yet in effect as on 30.04.2026, and pending a separate applicability announcement by ICAI for future examinations), section 15(3)(b) is proposed to be amended to do away with the requirement of linking the post-supply discount to a PRE-EXISTING agreement (at or before the time of supply) that is invoice-wise linkable. subject: Goods and Services Tax
question_html: Vibhuti Traders sells goods to a customer for a list price of Rs. 40,000 (exclusive of taxes and discounts). It separately charges Rs. 4,000 as tax levied by the Municipal Authority on the sale of such goods, and Rs. 800 as packing charges (not included in the list price). It has also received a price-linked subsidy of Rs. 1,600 from a non-Government body, already factored into arriving at the Rs. 40,000 list price. What is the value of taxable supply (before considering any discount)?

options.A: Rs. 44,000, excluding the non-Government subsidy on the basis that only Government subsidies are relevant to the value of supply computation
options.B: Rs. 40,800, excluding both the municipal tax and the subsidy, on the basis that only packing charges are includible incidental expenses
options.C: Rs. 46,400, but treating the subsidy as deductible from, rather than includible in, the value of supply since it reduces the price actually paid by the customer
options.D: Rs. 46,400 (Rs. 40,000 list price + Rs. 4,000 municipal tax [Section 15(2)(a)] + Rs. 800 packing charges [Section 15(2)(c)] + Rs. 1,600 non-Government subsidy directly linked to price [Section 15(2)(e)])

answer_html:
Correct answer: (D) Rs. 46,400 (Rs. 40,000 list price + Rs. 4,000 municipal tax [Section 15(2)(a)] + Rs. 800 packing charges [Section 15(2)(c)] + Rs. 1,600 non-Government subsidy directly linked to price [Section 15(2)(e)])

Municipal tax (a non-GST tax charged separately) is includible under section 15(2)(a); packing charges are includible under section 15(2)(c); and the subsidy from the non-Government body, being directly linked to price, is includible under section 15(2)(e). Total value of taxable supply = Rs. 40,000 + Rs. 4,000 + Rs. 800 + Rs. 1,600 = Rs. 46,400.

subject: Goods and Services Tax
question_html: Kavach Advertisers designs an advertising campaign for a client, Starline Retail Pvt. Ltd., for a consideration of Rs. 6,00,000. Kavach Advertisers owed Rs. 25,000 to one of its own vendors in relation to the advertising service provided to Starline Retail Pvt. Ltd.; this liability of Kavach Advertisers was directly discharged by Starline Retail Pvt. Ltd. (and was not billed by Kavach Advertisers). Ignoring any interest for delayed payment, what is the value of taxable supply made by Kavach Advertisers?

options.A: Rs. 6,25,000 (Rs. 6,00,000 service charges + Rs. 25,000 being the supplier's own liability discharged by the recipient, includible under section 15(2)(b))
options.B: Rs. 6,00,000, since the Rs. 25,000 was paid directly by Starline Retail Pvt. Ltd. to the vendor and was never billed by Kavach Advertisers, and is therefore outside the scope of the supply
options.C: Rs. 6,25,000, but treating the Rs. 25,000 as a subsidy directly linked to price under section 15(2)(e), rather than as a third-party payment under section 15(2)(b)
options.D: Rs. 5,75,000, treating the Rs. 25,000 as a permissible deduction/discount from the value of the advertising service

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) Rs. 6,25,000 (Rs. 6,00,000 service charges + Rs. 25,000 being the supplier's own liability discharged by the recipient, includible under section 15(2)(b))

Since Kavach Advertisers was liable to pay the Rs. 25,000 to its vendor in relation to the advertising service, but this liability was instead discharged directly by the recipient (Starline Retail Pvt. Ltd.), this amount is includible in the value of supply under section 15(2)(b), even though it was not billed by Kavach Advertisers itself. Value of taxable supply = Rs. 6,00,000 + Rs. 25,000 = Rs. 6,25,000.

question_html: Continuing the Kavach Advertisers/Starline Retail Pvt. Ltd. example above (base value Rs. 6,25,000), Starline Retail Pvt. Ltd. delayed payment of consideration and paid Rs. 18,000 as interest for the delay (assumed to be inclusive of GST at 18%). What is the amount includible in the value of supply on account of this interest, and what is the total value of taxable supply?

options.A: Interest includible = Rs. 18,000 (taken at face value without any back-calculation); total value of taxable supply = Rs. 6,43,000
options.B: Interest includible = Rs. 15,254 (Rs. 18,000 x 100/118, rounded off); total value of taxable supply = Rs. 6,40,254 (Rs. 6,25,000 + Rs. 15,254)
options.C: Interest includible = Rs. 21,240 (Rs. 18,000 grossed up by adding 18% GST rather than backing it out); total value of taxable supply = Rs. 6,46,240
options.D: Interest includible = NIL, since interest for delayed payment is excluded from the value of supply once the underlying service charges have already been fully valued

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) Interest includible = Rs. 15,254 (Rs. 18,000 x 100/118, rounded off); total value of taxable supply = Rs. 6,40,254 (Rs. 6,25,000 + Rs. 15,254)

Since the interest for delay in payment is assumed to be inclusive of GST at 18%, the value includible under section 15(2)(d) is computed by back-calculation: Rs. 18,000 x (100/118) = Rs. 15,254 (rounded off). Total value of taxable supply = Rs. 6,25,000 (base value) + Rs. 15,254 (interest) = Rs. 6,40,254.

subject: Goods and Services Tax
question_html: Meridian Devices Pvt. Ltd. sells goods to Colourtone Pvt. Ltd. The price of Rs. 60,000 charged (exclusive of taxes and discounts) is net of a price-linked subsidy of Rs. 2,500 received from an NGO. Meridian Devices Pvt. Ltd. also offers a 2% discount on the list price, duly recorded in the invoice for the goods. What is the value of taxable supply?

options.A: Rs. 58,800 (Rs. 60,000 less the 2% discount of Rs. 1,200 alone, excluding the non-Government subsidy from the computation entirely)
options.B: Rs. 62,500 (Rs. 60,000 plus the Rs. 2,500 subsidy, without allowing any deduction for the discount, on the basis that discounts are never deductible once a subsidy has been added to the value)
options.C: Rs. 61,300 (Rs. 60,000 price + Rs. 2,500 non-Government subsidy directly linked to price [Section 15(2)(e)] = Rs. 62,500; less 2% discount on Rs. 60,000 = Rs. 1,200, duly recorded in the invoice and deductible under section 15(3)(a); Rs. 62,500 - Rs. 1,200 = Rs. 61,300)
options.D: Rs. 61,300, but computed by first deducting the discount from Rs. 60,000 and then adding the full Rs. 2,500 subsidy without any adjustment, coincidentally arriving at the same figure through an incorrect method

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) Rs. 61,300 (Rs. 60,000 price + Rs. 2,500 non-Government subsidy directly linked to price [Section 15(2)(e)] = Rs. 62,500; less 2% discount on Rs. 60,000 = Rs. 1,200, duly recorded in the invoice and deductible under section 15(3)(a); Rs. 62,500 - Rs. 1,200 = Rs. 61,300)

Step 1: Since the price of Rs. 60,000 is net of the subsidy, the subsidy (Rs. 2,500, from a non-Government body, directly linked to price) must be added back under section 15(2)(e): Rs. 60,000 + Rs. 2,500 = Rs. 62,500. Step 2: The 2% discount on the list price (Rs. 60,000 x 2% = Rs. 1,200), being recorded in the invoice, is deductible under section 15(3)(a): Rs. 62,500 - Rs. 1,200 = Rs. 61,300, the value of taxable supply.

subject: Goods and Services Tax
question_html: Continuing a similar fact pattern: Shivalik Pvt. Ltd. sold goods to Parvat Pvt. Ltd., who paid Rs. 1,500 as late fees for delayed payment (inclusive of GST); however, Shivalik Pvt. Ltd. subsequently waived these late fees in full and refunded the Rs. 1,500 to Parvat Pvt. Ltd. within the same month. How should this Rs. 1,500 be treated while computing the value of taxable supply?

options.A: It shall be included in the value of supply at its full inclusive-of-GST amount, regardless of the subsequent waiver and refund, since it was collected at least once during the tax period
options.B: It shall be included in the value of supply, but only the back-calculated GST-exclusive portion, regardless of the subsequent waiver and refund
options.C: It shall be included in the value of supply, but treated as a separate residual supply under section 15(5), given the unusual waiver and refund
options.D: It shall NOT be included in the value of supply, since the late fee was ultimately waived off by Shivalik Pvt. Ltd. and refunded to Parvat Pvt. Ltd. - the supplier never actually 'received' the addition in value

answer_html:
Correct answer: (D) It shall NOT be included in the value of supply, since the late fee was ultimately waived off by Shivalik Pvt. Ltd. and refunded to Parvat Pvt. Ltd. - the supplier never actually 'received' the addition in value

Since interest/late fee/penalty is includible in the value of supply only when the supplier actually receives such addition in value [Section 15(2)(d)], and here the late fee was subsequently waived off in full and the amount refunded, it is NOT includible in the value of taxable supply - there is no addition in value that the supplier has ultimately retained/received.

subject: Goods and Services Tax
question_html: Anmol Pvt. Ltd. sells goods to Tarang Pvt. Ltd. for a price of Rs. 90,000 (exclusive of taxes), plus municipal tax of Rs. 1,800 (charged separately). Tarang Pvt. Ltd. also directly pays weighment charges of Rs. 1,500 to a third-party weighbridge operator, Sthir Weighing Co., on behalf of Anmol Pvt. Ltd. (this being Anmol Pvt. Ltd.'s own contractual liability, not recorded in Anmol Pvt. Ltd.'s invoice). What is the value of taxable supply made by Anmol Pvt. Ltd. to Tarang Pvt. Ltd.?

options.A: Rs. 93,300 (Rs. 90,000 price + Rs. 1,800 municipal tax [Section 15(2)(a)] + Rs. 1,500 weighment charges paid by the recipient on the supplier's behalf [Section 15(2)(b)])
options.B: Rs. 91,800, excluding the weighment charges, since they were paid directly by Tarang Pvt. Ltd. to Sthir Weighing Co. rather than to Anmol Pvt. Ltd.
options.C: Rs. 90,000, excluding both the municipal tax and the weighment charges, since neither was recorded in Anmol Pvt. Ltd.'s own invoice
options.D: Rs. 93,300, but treating the weighment charges as an exempt ancillary service provided by Sthir Weighing Co. directly to Tarang Pvt. Ltd., unrelated to Anmol Pvt. Ltd.'s value of supply

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) Rs. 93,300 (Rs. 90,000 price + Rs. 1,800 municipal tax [Section 15(2)(a)] + Rs. 1,500 weighment charges paid by the recipient on the supplier's behalf [Section 15(2)(b)])

Municipal tax charged separately is includible under section 15(2)(a). The weighment charges, being Anmol Pvt. Ltd.'s own contractual liability (to Sthir Weighing Co.) but directly discharged by the recipient Tarang Pvt. Ltd., are includible under section 15(2)(b), even though not recorded in Anmol Pvt. Ltd.'s invoice. Value of taxable supply = Rs. 90,000 + Rs. 1,800 + Rs. 1,500 = Rs. 93,300.

subject: Goods and Services Tax
question_html: Nabhganga Pvt. Ltd., Delhi, a registered supplier, makes an inter-State supply of taxable goods with a list price of Rs. 20,00,000 (exclusive of taxes). It receives a price-linked subsidy of Rs. 3,00,000 from the Central Government for supply of these goods to a Government school (this subsidy being exclusively related to this supply, and the list price being net of this subsidy). What amount, if any, should be added to the value of supply on account of this subsidy?

options.A: Rs. 3,00,000 should be added, since any price-linked subsidy directly related to a specific supply is includible in the value of supply regardless of its source
options.B: NIL - since the subsidy is received from the Central Government, it is NOT includible in the value of supply, as per section 15(2)(e)
options.C: Rs. 1,50,000 (50% of the subsidy) should be added, applying a proportionate inclusion rule for Government subsidies to specified categories of institutions
options.D: Rs. 3,00,000 should be added, but only because the subsidy is linked to supply to a Government school rather than to a private-sector recipient

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) NIL - since the subsidy is received from the Central Government, it is NOT includible in the value of supply, as per section 15(2)(e)

As per section 15(2)(e), the value of supply includes subsidies directly linked to the price, EXCLUDING subsidies provided by the Central Government and State Governments. Since this subsidy of Rs. 3,00,000 is from the Central Government, it is NOT includible in the value of supply, regardless of the fact that it is directly linked to price and relates to a specific supply.

subject: Goods and Services Tax
question_html: Continuing the Nabhganga Pvt. Ltd. example (list price Rs. 20,00,000, net of a Rs. 3,00,000 Central Government subsidy), Nabhganga Pvt. Ltd. also separately receives a price-linked subsidy of Rs. 75,000 from an NGO, exclusively related to the same supply of goods (also already factored into arriving at the Rs. 20,00,000 list price). What is the total value of the supply of goods, considering both subsidies?

options.A: Rs. 23,75,000, adding back both the Rs. 3,00,000 Central Government subsidy and the Rs. 75,000 NGO subsidy to the list price
options.B: Rs. 20,00,000, excluding both subsidies from the value of supply since both were already factored into arriving at the list price
options.C: Rs. 20,75,000 (Rs. 20,00,000 list price + Rs. 75,000 non-Government subsidy, directly linked to price, includible under section 15(2)(e); the Rs. 3,00,000 Central Government subsidy remains excluded)
options.D: Rs. 20,75,000, but arrived at by adding the Rs. 3,00,000 Government subsidy and excluding the Rs. 75,000 NGO subsidy, the reverse of the correct treatment

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) Rs. 20,75,000 (Rs. 20,00,000 list price + Rs. 75,000 non-Government subsidy, directly linked to price, includible under section 15(2)(e); the Rs. 3,00,000 Central Government subsidy remains excluded)

The Central Government subsidy of Rs. 3,00,000 remains excluded under section 15(2)(e). However, the Rs. 75,000 subsidy from the NGO (a non-Government body), being directly linked to price and already netted out of the list price, must be added back: Rs. 20,00,000 + Rs. 75,000 = Rs. 20,75,000, the value of supply of the goods.

subject: Goods and Services Tax
question_html: Prithvi Traders sells goods to an Old Age Home for a consideration of Rs. 1,50,000 (the normal sale value of such goods being Rs. 3,00,000). An NGO registered under section 12AB of the Income-tax Act, 1961 gives Prithvi Traders a subsidy of Rs. 45,000 to acknowledge its services to elderly people, but this subsidy is a general gesture of appreciation and is NOT directly linked to the price of the specific goods sold. What is the value of taxable supply?

options.A: Rs. 3,00,000, being the normal sale value of the goods, since GST is levied on the fair market value rather than the actual transaction price where a concessional price is charged to a charitable institution
options.B: Rs. 1,95,000, adding the full NGO subsidy of Rs. 45,000 to the transaction value of Rs. 1,50,000, regardless of whether the subsidy is directly linked to price
options.C: Rs. 2,25,000, being the average of the transaction value of Rs. 1,50,000 and the normal sale value of Rs. 3,00,000
options.D: Rs. 1,50,000, being the transaction value (price actually paid or payable) - the NGO subsidy of Rs. 45,000 is not includible since it is not directly linked to the price of the goods, and the 'normal sale value' of Rs. 3,00,000 is irrelevant since section 15(1) looks to the actual transaction price, not a notional market value

answer_html:
Correct answer: (D) Rs. 1,50,000, being the transaction value (price actually paid or payable) - the NGO subsidy of Rs. 45,000 is not includible since it is not directly linked to the price of the goods, and the 'normal sale value' of Rs. 3,00,000 is irrelevant since section 15(1) looks to the actual transaction price, not a notional market value

Under section 15(1), the transaction value is the value of supply where price is the sole consideration and the parties are unrelated - this is Rs. 1,50,000, irrespective of the 'normal sale value'. The NGO subsidy of Rs. 45,000 is not includible under section 15(2)(e) since it is a blanket/general subsidy and not directly linked to the price of the goods being valued. Therefore, the value of taxable supply is Rs. 1,50,000.

subject: Goods and Services Tax
question_html: Under a contract with the State Government, Bhoomi Agro Supplies sells 500 units of goods (unit price Rs. 600 per unit) at a concessional Rs. 350 per unit to families of an identified Economic Weaker Section category, with the balance Rs. 250 per unit to be paid to Bhoomi Agro Supplies by the State Government as a subsidy. What is the value of taxable supply of these 500 units?

options.A: Rs. 1,75,000 (500 units x Rs. 350 per unit, being the price actually paid by the EWS families) - the State Government subsidy of Rs. 250 per unit is NOT includible in the value of supply under section 15(2)(e)
options.B: Rs. 3,00,000 (500 units x Rs. 600 per unit), treating the subsidy as includible in the value of supply since it is directly and specifically linked to the price of each unit sold
options.C: Rs. 1,25,000 (500 units x Rs. 250 per unit), treating only the State Government subsidy component itself as the value of taxable supply
options.D: Rs. 1,75,000, but only because the recipients are individually identified Economic Weaker Section families rather than a general body of consumers

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) Rs. 1,75,000 (500 units x Rs. 350 per unit, being the price actually paid by the EWS families) - the State Government subsidy of Rs. 250 per unit is NOT includible in the value of supply under section 15(2)(e)

Even though the State Government subsidy of Rs. 250 per unit is directly linked to the price of the goods, section 15(2)(e) expressly EXCLUDES subsidies given by the State Government from the value of supply. Therefore, the value of taxable supply is based only on the price actually paid by the EWS families: 500 units x Rs. 350 = Rs. 1,75,000.

subject: Goods and Services Tax
question_html: Charan Enterprises sold 2,000 units of goods to Udaan Distributors at Rs. 350 each. Under the Income Tax Act, Charan Enterprises was required to collect tax (TCS) of Rs. 3,500 from Udaan Distributors, and included this Rs. 3,500 as TCS in the tax invoice issued to Udaan Distributors. What is the value of taxable supply on which Charan Enterprises must pay GST, in respect of this transaction?

options.A: Rs. 7,03,500 (2,000 units x Rs. 350, plus the Rs. 3,500 TCS), since any amount included in the tax invoice, including TCS, forms part of the value of supply under section 15(2)(a)
options.B: Rs. 7,00,000 (2,000 units x Rs. 350), EXCLUDING the Rs. 3,500 TCS, since TCS under the Income-tax Act is not includible in the value of supply for GST purposes as clarified vide Circular No. 76/50/2018 GST (it being an interim levy not having the character of a tax)
options.C: Rs. 7,00,000, but this is coincidental, since TCS would ordinarily be includible under section 15(2)(a) as a tax levied under a law other than the GST laws, charged separately
options.D: Rs. 3,500, being only the TCS amount, treated as a separate and distinct taxable supply of a tax-collection service

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) Rs. 7,00,000 (2,000 units x Rs. 350), EXCLUDING the Rs. 3,500 TCS, since TCS under the Income-tax Act is not includible in the value of supply for GST purposes as clarified vide Circular No. 76/50/2018 GST (it being an interim levy not having the character of a tax)

As clarified vide Circular No. 76/50/2018 GST dated 31.12.2018, TCS under the Income-tax Act, 1961 would NOT be includible in the value of supply for GST purposes, as it is an interim levy not having the character of a tax - this is despite the fact that it was included in the tax invoice. Therefore, the value of taxable supply is Rs. 7,00,000 (2,000 x Rs. 350), excluding the Rs. 3,500 TCS.

subject: Goods and Services Tax
question_html: Mezda Banners, an advertising firm, gives its customers an interest-free credit period of 30 days for payment. Its customer ABC paid for a supply 32 days after the supply of service. Mezda Banners waived the interest payable for the delay of two days. Should notional interest for the two-day delay be added to the value of supply, even though it was waived and never received?

options.A: Yes - since the terms of the arrangement technically permitted Mezda Banners to charge interest for the two-day delay, the value of supply must include such notional interest regardless of the waiver
options.B: Yes - but only to the extent of one day's interest, applying a 50% notional inclusion as a reasonable compromise between the full waiver and the technically permissible interest
options.C: No - since interest/late fee/penalty is includible in the value of supply only when the supplier actually RECEIVES such addition in value [Section 15(2)(d)], and Mezda Banners has waived (and thus not received) the interest for the two-day delay, no notional interest is to be added
options.D: No - but only because the delay was of two days or less; had the delay exceeded a week, notional interest would need to be included regardless of any waiver

answer_html:

question_html: Crunch Bakery Products Ltd. sells biscuits and cakes through dealers at the list price minus a standard discount, and pays GST accordingly. When goods remain unsold with dealers, it offers additional discounts on the unsold stock as an incentive to push sales, WITHOUT any prior agreement between the parties for such additional discount. Can this additional discount be deducted from the value of supply, with corresponding GST adjustments made?

options.A: Yes - any discount offered by a supplier to push sales of unsold stock is automatically deductible from the value of supply, regardless of whether it was agreed at the time of the original supply

subject: Goods and Services Tax
question_html: Precision Tools Ltd. manufactures and sells a customised industrial lathe machine for Rs. 12,00,000. Before delivering the machine, Precision Tools conducts a mandatory quality-testing and calibration process at its own factory (as required under the buyer's purchase specifications) and separately bills the buyer Rs. 40,000 for this testing/calibration, in addition to the machine price. Is the Rs. 40,000 testing charge includible in the value of supply, and if so, what is the total taxable value?

options.A: Yes, the Rs. 40,000 is includible under section 15(2)(c), since the testing/calibration is performed by Precision Tools itself, in relation to the machine, before its delivery to the buyer; the total taxable value is Rs. 12,40,000, regardless of whether it is billed as a separate line item
options.B: No, the Rs. 40,000 is excludible, since it is billed as a distinct, separately-stated line item on the invoice rather than being embedded within the machine's base price
options.C: Yes, but only 50% of the Rs. 40,000 is includible, with the remainder being treated as a separate, independently taxable supply of testing services at a different GST rate
options.D: No, the Rs. 40,000 is excludible, since mandatory pre-delivery testing required by the buyer's own purchase specifications is treated as a distinct statutory compliance cost outside the scope of section 15(2)(c)

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) Yes, the Rs. 40,000 is includible under section 15(2)(c), since the testing/calibration is performed by Precision Tools itself, in relation to the machine, before its delivery to the buyer; the total taxable value is Rs. 12,40,000, regardless of whether it is billed as a separate line item

subject: Goods and Services Tax
question_html: Which of the following best captures the correct legal position on whether 'consideration' under GST law can include non-monetary elements, with reference to the definition under section 2(31)?

options.A: Consideration under GST law is restricted exclusively to payments made in money (Indian legal tender or foreign currency), with any non-monetary element being entirely disregarded for valuation purposes
options.B: Consideration under GST law includes both monetary and non-monetary considerations - it takes within its sweep the monetary value of any act or forbearance, by the recipient or any other person, for the supply, in addition to payment made or to be made in money or otherwise
options.C: Consideration under GST law includes non-monetary elements only where the supply is made between related persons, with unrelated-person transactions being valued exclusively on a monetary basis under section 15(1)
options.D: Consideration under GST law includes non-monetary elements only where they are reduced to a written valuation report certified by a registered valuer prior to the time of supply

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) Consideration under GST law includes both monetary and non-monetary considerations - it takes within its sweep the monetary value of any act or forbearance, by the recipient or any other person, for the supply, in addition to payment made or to be made in money or otherwise

As per the definition of 'consideration' under section 2(31), consideration includes both payment in money or otherwise made by the recipient or any other person, and also takes within its sweep the monetary value of any act or forbearance, by the recipient or any other person, for the supply. Further, it includes a deposit that is applied as consideration but excludes subsidies from the State/Central Government. Non-monetary consideration essentially means consideration in kind, and the statement that consideration includes both monetary and non-monetary elements is therefore correct.

case_facts_html: Suvidha Textiles Ltd. manufactures and sells taxable fabric. In Transaction 1, it supplies fabric to a Government-run vocational training centre at a concessional price, with the list price of Rs. 12,00,000 (exclusive of taxes) being net of a price-linked subsidy of Rs. 1,80,000 received from the State Government, exclusively related to this supply. In Transaction 2, Suvidha Textiles Ltd. separately supplies fabric to a private charitable trust, with the list price of Rs. 6,00,000 (exclusive of taxes) being net of a price-linked subsidy of Rs. 40,000 received from an NGO, Sahayog Foundation, exclusively related to this supply. In Transaction 3, Suvidha Textiles Ltd. receives a blanket, lump-sum donation of Rs. 2,50,000 from a corporate sponsor, Mahesh Industries Foundation, as general goodwill support unrelated to the price of any specific supply, alongside its regular sale of fabric worth Rs. 9,00,000 (exclusive of taxes) to an unrelated buyer.
question_html: What is the value of taxable supply for Transaction 1?

options.A: Rs. 13,80,000, adding back the State Government subsidy of Rs. 1,80,000 to the list price, since it is directly linked to the price of the specific supply
options.B: Rs. 10,20,000, deducting the State Government subsidy of Rs. 1,80,000 from the list price, treating it as a discount rather than as excludible consideration
options.C: Rs. 12,00,000, being the list price alone - the State Government subsidy of Rs. 1,80,000 is NOT includible in the value of supply, as per section 15(2)(e)
options.D: Rs. 12,00,000, but only because the recipient is a Government-run institution rather than because of the source of the subsidy

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) Rs. 12,00,000, being the list price alone - the State Government subsidy of Rs. 1,80,000 is NOT includible in the value of supply, as per section 15(2)(e)

As per section 15(2)(e), subsidies provided by the Central Government or a State Government are expressly excluded from the value of supply, regardless of whether they are directly linked to price. Since the list price of Rs. 12,00,000 is already net of the State Government subsidy, no further adjustment (addition) is required, and the value of taxable supply remains Rs. 12,00,000.

options.A: Rs. 9,00,000, being the transaction value of the fabric sold - the Rs. 2,50,000 blanket donation from Mahesh Industries Foundation is NOT includible, since it is a general goodwill contribution not directly linked to the price of this or any specific supply
options.B: Rs. 11,50,000, adding the entire Rs. 2,50,000 donation to the value of the fabric supply, since any receipt from a non-Government body is automatically includible under section 15(2)(e)
options.C: Rs. 9,00,000, but only coincidentally, since the donation should properly be apportioned across all of Suvidha Textiles Ltd.'s supplies made during the relevant period

case_facts_html: Vibrant Electronics sold goods to three different customers during the month. In Sale 1, it sold 500 units at Rs. 800 each to Kunal Retail Mart, and was required under the Income Tax Act to collect TCS of Rs. 4,000 from Kunal Retail Mart, which it duly included as a separate line item in its tax invoice. In Sale 2, it sold goods worth Rs. 3,00,000 (exclusive of taxes) to Bhairav Distributors, and separately charged Rs. 15,000 as entry tax levied by a local municipal authority on the sale of such goods (charged separately by Vibrant Electronics and shown as a distinct line item in the invoice). In Sale 3, it sold goods worth Rs. 2,50,000 (exclusive of taxes) to Aarohi Traders, and this price already included, without separate disclosure, an amount of Rs. 8,000 that Vibrant Electronics had itself borne as octroi payable on the goods (i.e. this octroi was factored into the Rs. 2,50,000 price rather than charged as a distinct, separate amount).
question_html: What is the value of taxable supply for Sale 1 (Kunal Retail Mart)?

options.A: Rs. 4,04,000, including the Rs. 4,000 TCS, since it was charged separately by Vibrant Electronics and shown as a distinct line item in the invoice, mirroring the treatment of other non-GST taxes under section 15(2)(a)
options.B: Rs. 4,000, being only the TCS amount, treated as a separate and distinct taxable supply of a collection/administrative service
options.C: Rs. 4,00,000, but only because Kunal Retail Mart is described as a 'Retail Mart' rather than because of the specific nature of TCS as an interim levy
options.D: Rs. 4,00,000 (500 units x Rs. 800), EXCLUDING the Rs. 4,000 TCS - as clarified vide Circular No. 76/50/2018 GST, TCS under the Income-tax Act is not includible in the value of supply, being an interim levy not having the character of a tax, even though it was separately shown in the invoice

answer_html:
Correct answer: (D) Rs. 4,00,000 (500 units x Rs. 800), EXCLUDING the Rs. 4,000 TCS - as clarified vide Circular No. 76/50/2018 GST, TCS under the Income-tax Act is not includible in the value of supply, being an interim levy not having the character of a tax, even though it was separately shown in the invoice

Even though TCS was charged separately and shown as a distinct line item (which would ordinarily suggest inclusion under section 15(2)(a), like other non-GST taxes), the CBIC has specifically clarified via Circular No. 76/50/2018 GST that TCS under the Income-tax Act is NOT includible in the value of supply, as it is merely an interim levy (an advance collection mechanism) and does not have the character of a tax. The value of taxable supply is therefore Rs. 4,00,000 (500 x Rs. 800), excluding the TCS.

subject: Goods and Services Tax
case_facts_html: SafeGuard General Insurance issues a motor insurance policy to Mr. Yuvraj Deol, with a gross annual premium of Rs. 18,000. As per the policy document (which discloses the availability of a No Claim Bonus, or NCB, subject to conditions), Mr. Deol is entitled to an NCB of Rs. 3,600 for having made no claims in the preceding policy year; this NCB is specifically mentioned and deducted in the invoice/premium receipt issued to him. Separately, SafeGuard General Insurance also offers Ms. Tanvi Chawla, another policyholder, an ad hoc, goodwill 'loyalty reduction' of Rs. 1,200 on her Rs. 15,000 premium, decided at the time of renewal purely at the discretion of the branch manager, with no mention of any such reduction in the original policy document, and this reduction is conveyed to Ms. Chawla only via a separate covering letter, not through the premium invoice itself.
question_html: What is the key legal distinction, per Circular No. 186/18/2022 GST, between the treatment of Mr. Deol's NCB and a purely commercial/financial reduction such as Ms. Chawla's loyalty reduction (assuming, for Ms. Chawla, that SafeGuard General Insurance later issues only a commercial credit note for the Rs. 1,200, without any GST component)?

options.A: NCB satisfying section 15(3)(a) directly reduces the taxable value of supply (with GST leviable only on the net premium after NCB), whereas a purely commercial credit note (with no GST) issued for an ad hoc reduction like Ms. Chawla's has no legal effect on the value of supply for GST purposes - the recipient is not required to reverse any ITC, and correspondingly the insurer cannot reduce its own GST liability using such a note
options.B: There is no legal distinction at all; both NCB and any commercial credit note issued by an insurer have an identical effect of directly reducing the taxable value of the insurance premium
options.C: The distinction is that NCB applies only to motor insurance policies, whereas commercial credit notes may be issued for any class of insurance product, regardless of the disclosure conditions
options.D: The distinction is that NCB is available only to policyholders renewing for a second consecutive year, whereas commercial credit notes may be issued to first-time policyholders as well

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) NCB satisfying section 15(3)(a) directly reduces the taxable value of supply (with GST leviable only on the net premium after NCB), whereas a purely commercial credit note (with no GST) issued for an ad hoc reduction like Ms. Chawla's has no legal effect on the value of supply for GST purposes - the recipient is not required to reverse any ITC, and correspondingly the insurer cannot reduce its own GST liability using such a note

The key distinction lies in whether the section 15(3)(a) conditions are satisfied: NCB, being pre-disclosed in the policy document and specifically recorded in the invoice, qualifies as a valid discount under section 15(3)(a), directly reducing the taxable value (GST payable on the net premium). A purely commercial/financial credit note (as would be issued for Ms. Chawla's undisclosed, ad hoc reduction) is NOT governed by GST law, carries no GST component, does not require any ITC reversal by the recipient, and does not entitle the insurer to reduce its own output tax liability - it has no bearing on the value of supply for GST purposes.

subject: Goods and Services Tax
case_facts_html: Everest Industrial Supplies sells a batch of industrial equipment to Zenway Manufacturing Ltd. The relevant particulars are: price of the equipment (exclusive of taxes and other charges/discounts) is Rs. 5,00,000; Everest Industrial Supplies separately charges Rs. 25,000 as entry tax levied by a local authority on the sale of such equipment; packing charges of Rs. 8,000 (not included in the price above) are separately charged; Everest Industrial Supplies receives a price-linked subsidy of Rs. 40,000 from the State Government (already netted out of the Rs. 5,00,000 price); Zenway Manufacturing Ltd. directly pays Rs. 12,000 to a third-party calibration agency on Everest Industrial Supplies' behalf, this being Everest Industrial Supplies' own contractual liability and not recorded in its invoice; and Everest Industrial Supplies offers a discount of 2% on the equipment price of Rs. 5,00,000, duly recorded in the invoice.
question_html: Which of the following correctly identifies how EACH of the five additional elements (entry tax, packing charges, State Government subsidy, third-party calibration payment, and 2% discount) should be treated in computing the value of taxable supply?

options.A: State Government subsidy (Rs. 40,000) - must be added back to the price under section 15(2)(e), being treated on par with the non-Government subsidy in Illustration 1 of the Study Material; all other elements treated as in the correct answer
options.B: Entry tax (Rs. 25,000) - includible [Section 15(2)(a)]; packing charges (Rs. 8,000) - includible [Section 15(2)(c)]; State Government subsidy (Rs. 40,000) - NOT includible/no adjustment needed since it is already netted out and excluded under section 15(2)(e); third-party calibration payment (Rs. 12,000) - includible [Section 15(2)(b)]; 2% discount - deductible [Section 15(3)(a)]
options.C: Third-party calibration payment (Rs. 12,000) - excluded from the value of supply since it was paid directly to the calibration agency and not to Everest Industrial Supplies; all other elements treated as in the correct answer
options.D: 2% discount - NOT deductible from the value of supply since it is a percentage-based discount rather than a fixed-amount discount; all other elements treated as in the correct answer

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) Entry tax (Rs. 25,000) - includible [Section 15(2)(a)]; packing charges (Rs. 8,000) - includible [Section 15(2)(c)]; State Government subsidy (Rs. 40,000) - NOT includible/no adjustment needed since it is already netted out and excluded under section 15(2)(e); third-party calibration payment (Rs. 12,000) - includible [Section 15(2)(b)]; 2% discount - deductible [Section 15(3)(a)]

Entry tax, being a non-GST tax charged separately, is includible under section 15(2)(a). Packing charges are includible under section 15(2)(c). The State Government subsidy is EXCLUDED under section 15(2)(e) (and since the price is already net of it, no further adjustment is needed - it is simply not added back, unlike a non-Government subsidy which WOULD need to be added back). The calibration payment, being Everest Industrial Supplies' own liability discharged by the recipient, is includible under section 15(2)(b). The 2% discount, recorded in the invoice at the time of supply, is deductible under section 15(3)(a).

options.C: Rs. 5,25,000, incorrectly deducting a flat Rs. 20,000 rather than the correctly computed 2% of Rs. 5,00,000, i.e. Rs. 10,000
